solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Country retreat houses a minister

indicators.note: a building that houses something holds it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: country as an adjective, of the countryside
a den is a private hideaway

explanation.surface: A cottage hideaway in the countryside is home to a clergyman seeking peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country retreat' reads as one idea, a cottage, but splits into two pieces with the A tucked inside the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A rural dean is a Church of England cleric who supervises a group of parishes, so is a minister.

clue.text: Leaders for reasons obscure bankrupt firm

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their opening letters, taken from the next two words

blocks.note: the opening letters of each word

explanation.surface: Top people give murky reasons why a company went under.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm' looks like a noun after 'bankrupt', but it is the adjective defining the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Robust means strong and sturdy, the sense of firm as solid and steady.

clue.text: Soldiers turn up worried about one visiting dangerous territory

indicators.note: in a down clue turning something up flips it so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: as in 'what's eating you?': something that ate at you worried you

explanation.surface: Troops arrive anxious about a visitor to a hostile land.
explanation.walkthrough: OR, other ranks, is the usual crossword abbreviation for ordinary soldiers; 'worried about' works like 'ate at', as anxiety eats at you.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogue state is a nation seen as lawless and a threat to world peace, so a dangerous territory.

clue.text: Very funny fat boy's latest heretical ideas

indicators.note: the latest part of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: text shorthand for laughing out loud

explanation.surface: A tubby lad's newest notions are hilarious and unorthodox.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lollards were followers of John Wycliffe, condemned as heretics in 14th- and 15th-century England.
explanation.definitionFit: Lollardy is the body of Lollard doctrine, which the medieval Church judged heresy.

clue.text: Relaxed and stopped, taking hat off

indicators.note: a hat sits on top, so taking it off removes the topmost letter of this down entry

explanation.surface: Someone loosened up and paused to remove their hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Eased means loosened or lessened tension, the same as relaxed in the past tense.

clue.text: Disgusted as Edward accepts gold throne

indicators.note: someone who accepts something takes it in, so it goes inside

blocks.note: a throne is a seat of state

explanation.surface: A man is sickened when Edward takes a golden throne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edward' tempts toward the familiar two-letter short form, but a different pet name for Edward is the one that wraps the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Nauseated means made sick, and figuratively revolted, which is to be disgusted.

clue.text: Emperor we're told grants audience to a king

indicators.note: what we are told is heard by ear rather than read

blocks.note: to grant an audience is to see someone; a and R for rex, king

explanation.surface: An emperor reportedly receives a visiting monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: SEES A R, said quickly, matches the Roman name; R is Rex, Latin for king.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar became the title of Roman emperors after Julius Caesar, so Caesar names an emperor.

clue.text: Measure of warmth with a classical garment

blocks.note: the tog is a unit rating the insulation of duvets

explanation.surface: A warm-rated ancient robe.
explanation.definitionFit: The toga was the draped woollen robe worn by citizens of ancient Rome.

clue.text: I want to gaze at this reflection

definitions.text: I want to gaze at this

blocks.clueFragment: I want to gaze at this
blocks.note: first meaning: a request to look at something
second meaning: a phrase said while pausing to think

explanation.surface: Someone wishes to stare at their image in a mirror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflection' suggests a mirror, which fits gazing; it means thinking aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase both asks to look at something and serves as a filler while pondering, a moment of thought.

clue.text: Seafood and a US sausage (not Yankee)

indicators.note: Yankee is the radio alphabet word for its letter, and not means that letter is dropped

blocks.note: an American spelling of bologna sausage

explanation.surface: A menu offers seafood alongside an American sausage, with the Yankee bit removed.
explanation.walkthrough: Baloney, the US name for bologna sausage, loses its Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Abalone is an edible sea snail prized as a delicacy, a kind of seafood.

clue.text: Silly laughter? A measure of gravity becomes British pilot

indicators.note: one letter turns into another, swapping a single letter of the first word

blocks.note: g is the symbol for acceleration due to gravity

explanation.surface: Someone giggling turns into a stiff British airman.
explanation.walkthrough: The first G of the laughter word is replaced by B.
explanation.definitionFit: Biggles is the fictional flying ace of W. E. Johns's boys' adventure books, a famous pilot.

clue.text: One played loudly once as playwright married

blocks.note: George Bernard Shaw, the Irish dramatist

explanation.surface: A performer remembers being played loud back when a dramatist got married.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One played' looks like a person, but it is an instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The shawm is a loud medieval and Renaissance reed instrument, the forerunner of the oboe, so one played loudly in the past.

clue.text: Buzz off, small fly! Gone off

indicators.note: the abbreviation convention takes only the opening letter of this word

blocks.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small
a ked is a bloodsucking fly, as in the sheep ked
to addle is to go rotten, as an egg does

explanation.surface: Someone shoos away a little insect, and it is gone.
explanation.walkthrough: ADDLE strictly means go off rather than gone off, a looseness the blog noted.
explanation.definitionFit: Skedaddle is slang for leave in a hurry, the same command as buzz off.

clue.text: A medical procedure, in plain language not entirely relevant

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside its letters
a word not given in full loses its final letter

blocks.note: ordinary writing as opposed to verse

explanation.surface: A surgery explained in plain words is only partly to the point.
explanation.walkthrough: PROSE drops its E and the operation goes inside it, after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Apropos means pertinent or to the point, from the French for 'to the purpose'.

clue.text: In epidemic, exercise discretion about temperature

indicators.note: one word placed about another wraps around it

explanation.surface: During an outbreak, keep quiet about the temperature.
explanation.walkthrough: PE, physical education, is the usual crossword exercise; the temperature goes into the discretion word just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Pestilence is a deadly epidemic disease such as plague.

clue.text: Take out of container in garage

blocks.note: first meaning: to remove a plant from its pot
second meaning: a place where buses or vehicles are kept

explanation.surface: Someone unloads a box in the garage.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first meaning as DE-POT, the opposite of potting a seedling.
explanation.definitionFit: A depot is a storage yard or bus garage, and to depot a plant is to take it from its pot.

clue.text: One studying carefully about to call for dish

indicators.note: one word placed about another goes around it

explanation.surface: A scholar is about to phone for a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'about' wraps and 'to call' is the inner piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A porringer is a small bowl with a handle, used for porridge or soup, so a dish.

clue.text: Tedious year following sport

indicators.note: something following comes after, so the year's piece is placed behind the sport word

blocks.note: to sport clothes is to wear them

explanation.surface: A dull year in which nothing but sport happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' puts the year's letter after the sport word; 'sport' is a verb here, not games.
explanation.definitionFit: Weary can describe something tiresome and wearisome, as in a weary journey, matching tedious.

clue.text: Natural disaster that may be rife

blocks.clueFragment: Natural disaster that may be rife
blocks.note: surface reading: a catastrophe that may become widespread
setter's reading: the answer split into two words is an instruction to jumble four letters, and jumbling them can give the word rife

explanation.surface: Some natural catastrophe threatens to become widespread.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse anagram: read the answer as an instruction, the second word made 'wild', and it produces the clue's last word.
explanation.definitionFit: An uncontrolled blaze in forest or bush is a natural disaster that spreads rapidly.

clue.text: Paper which the head's left for children

indicators.note: the head has departed, so the leading letter is gone

explanation.surface: A newspaper the headteacher has abandoned, meant for the pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper' tempts as the definition, since an issue is a newspaper edition; it is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue is a legal and old word for offspring, as in 'died without issue'.

clue.text: Puzzle, urgent one I must crack

indicators.note: cracking something breaks it apart so the pieces can be reassembled differently

explanation.surface: A pressing riddle that someone simply has to solve.
explanation.definitionFit: To intrigue is to puzzle or arouse curiosity, verb to verb.

clue.text: A social event among the fleet is a gas

indicators.note: something among the others is surrounded by them

explanation.surface: A party held among sailors turns out to be a hoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a gas' slangily means great fun, which is the surface sense; here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Radon is a radioactive noble gas, chemical element 86.

clue.text: Frightening to break both hands? Should be more cautious

indicators.note: breaking into something means lying inside it, between its sides

explanation.surface: A scary prospect of breaking both hands should make one warier.
explanation.walkthrough: Both hands give L and R, the left and right, which go either side of EERIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Leery means wary or suspicious, so leerier is its comparative, warier.

clue.text: Spoil one's appearance: quietly going inside

indicators.note: something going inside enters between the other letters

blocks.note: one is I, so one's is I'M
p for piano, the musical direction for soft
an air is a manner or look

explanation.surface: Quietly sneaking in ruins somebody's looks.
explanation.walkthrough: P drops between the two other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To impair is to damage or weaken something, much like spoiling it.

clue.text: Bully's outwardly terribly strong words

indicators.note: only the outside of the word counts, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A bully's outward manner is full of fierce language.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyrant is an oppressive ruler or domineering person, which is what a bully is.

clue.text: Without scruple I will take Maoism to extremes in speech

indicators.note: only the two ends of the word are used, its outermost letters

explanation.surface: A speaker vows to push Mao's ideology to the extreme in their speeches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in speech' looks like a sound-alike signal but simply means ORALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting immorally is acting without moral scruples, the adverb matching the phrase.

clue.text: A doctor breaks into another dance

indicators.note: a burglar breaking into a house ends up inside it

explanation.surface: A doctor gatecrashes someone else's dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' reads as another dance, but it means another doctor, the medical officer of the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: The mambo is a Cuban ballroom dance.

clue.text: Place provided back in frame

indicators.note: going back means the letters are read from right to left

explanation.surface: Instructions to slot something back into a picture frame, if it fits.
explanation.definitionFit: To fit someone up is British slang for incriminating them falsely, which is also to frame them.

clue.text: A little drunk, almost overturns

indicators.note: almost the whole word means its final letter is missing

explanation.surface: Someone a bit tiddly nearly falls over.
explanation.definitionFit: To tip something is to tilt it so it falls, i.e. to upset or overturn it.

clue.text: Spy on Frenchman before a battle

explanation.surface: An instruction to keep watch on a Frenchman before a battle begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' here just places the spy next to the Frenchman; M for Monsieur is a standard French abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Magenta in Lombardy was the site of the 1859 battle in which France and Sardinia defeated Austria; the dye colour is named after it.

clue.text: Repeat "Company, stand!"

blocks.note: to stand up is to rise

explanation.surface: A sergeant major barks the order again for the company to stand.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a parade-ground command, but the quoted words are just the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprise is a repetition, especially of a musical passage, matching the noun repeat.

clue.text: Resolve to free Teddy

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order to be arranged anew

explanation.surface: Someone determines to release a teddy bear.
explanation.walkthrough: The teddy bear is named after this president.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodore Roosevelt, US president, was nicknamed Teddy, the origin of the teddy bear.
